# Can Wheels Become Unaligned After Replacing Struts?

It is entirely plausible for your steering wheel to sit off-center after a strut and mount replacement, even if the tie rods were never touched. This phenomenon often confuses DIY enthusiasts because the physical connection points of the suspension components remain unchanged, yet the vehicle's geometry has effectively shifted. The issue isn't necessarily that the alignment "went wrong" during installation; rather, it is highly likely that the wheels were actually misaligned *before* the repair and only now that you have a stable platform to notice it, the discrepancy is visible.

When you install new strut mounts or replace the entire strut assembly, you are fundamentally altering the vertical height of the suspension at that wheel hub. Strut mounts sit between the spring and the top of the strut shaft. If these were worn, they could allow for slight flex or tilt in the upper control arm mounting point. Replacing them with rigid new units restores the intended geometry, but it does not automatically correct lateral toe or caster settings established by the rest of the suspension system.

Consider the mechanics: if your vehicle previously sat on worn mounts that allowed a subtle tilt, the camber and potentially the toe angle relative to the ground might have been compromised in a way that felt normal during driving because the driver compensates for it subconsciously. Once you install new hardware, the wheel sits perfectly upright relative to the strut shaft, but if the tie rods were never adjusted to center the steering wheel while doing so, you are left with a vehicle that handles well but points slightly left or right when driving straight.

The specific scenario described in your case—replacing mounts on an Mk1 Golf/Rabbit Cabriolet—is particularly relevant because convertible chassis often experience more flex and wear in their suspension bushings compared to hardtop equivalents. If the old mounts had degraded significantly, they may have been masking a pre-existing alignment issue caused by body roll or frame settling. By stiffening that connection point, you exposed the underlying geometric error without correcting it.

To resolve this, you need a professional wheel alignment service. The technician will not adjust the struts themselves; instead, they will manipulate the tie rod ends (for toe adjustment) and potentially adjust camber shims or eccentric bolts depending on your specific chassis design. On many front-wheel-drive platforms like the Mk1 Golf, caster is often fixed by the strut assembly angle itself. If you installed a complete strut kit that included a different caster angle than what was removed, this could also contribute to the steering wheel offset, though less commonly than toe issues.

It is crucial to understand that replacing suspension components is not a "set and forget" maintenance item regarding alignment. Always verify the steering wheel centering after any work involving the strut assembly or tie rods. If you are comfortable with diagnostics but lack an alignment rack, measure the distance from the driver's side door edge to the passenger side hub cap at rest; if these distances differ significantly, your toe is likely off-center.

For those managing fleet maintenance or vehicle logistics where suspension repairs are frequent, ensuring that alignment verification is part of the standard operating procedure prevents unnecessary wear on tires and reduces driver fatigue caused by constant steering corrections. While the immediate fix requires a shop visit to adjust the tie rods, understanding *why* it happened helps prevent panic over potential theft or accidental damage to components that were actually never touched.
